11633-parsifal-a-mystical-drama-by-richa:
Oliver Huckel retells Wagner's Parsifal in the spirit of the Bayreuth interpretation, in three parts: the coming of Parsifal, the tempting of Parsifal, and the crowning of Parsifal. A castle rises in mountain woods above a smiling lake, home of the knights of the Holy Grail.

Kundry laughs and groans, Klingsor speaks of wounded knights, and a youth stands proud on garden walls, roses laughing in his cheeks. The retelling, published by Crowell, keeps Wagner's music drama in English verse and prose, with pictures of Monsalvat, the Grail communion, and Parsifal healing Amfortas.
1713-lincoln-an-account-of-his-personal-:
Nathaniel Wright Stephenson writes a life of Abraham Lincoln that stays close to the man rather than the monument. It traces his youth in Illinois, his law practice, and his marriage before the presidency. Notes and a bibliography back the main claims, and disputed points are argued in the notes instead of smoothed over.

The heart of the book is Lincoln under the strain of the Civil War: his melancholy, his belief in dreams and signs, and the way responsibility deepened rather than hardened him. Readers looking for Lincoln's character — patient, superstitious in his own way, and haunted by the war's cost — will find it in letters and the testimony of those near him.
24926-in-the-mahdi-s-grasp:
George Manville Fenn wrote In the Mahdi's Grasp about a young army officer held as a slave in the Sudan, long thought dead. His friends in London, one a skilled surgeon, sail to Cairo and push south, winning trust by cures and winning the ear of an influential sheikh. Their goal is the missing Harry, held in the Mahdi's stronghold.

Harry breaks his own arm so he can be brought to the surgeon, the Hakim, for treatment, and the party at last escapes with him straight through a battle. Their manservant, stained dark in disguise, nearly dies on the field. Fenn keeps the tension high through a long, informative tale of rescue in the Sudan wars.
27571-christianity-and-greek-philosophy-:
B. F. Cocker, professor of moral and mental philosophy at the University of Michigan, published this study in New York, San Francisco, and Cincinnati in 1870. Its full title states its theme: the relation between spontaneous and reflective thought in Greece and the positive teaching of Christ and his apostles.

Cocker takes Augustine's saying as epigraph: Plato revealed the true God, while Christ showed the way to him. He writes to deepen faith by showing that Christian truth rests not solely on special facts, but on all the facts of nature and humanity. The volume joins Greek philosophy and Christian teaching in one argument.
29068-an-introductorie-for-to-lerne-to-r:
Giles Du Wes, also called Du Guez, wrote this introduction for learning to read, pronounce, and speak French truly, compiled for the Lady Mary of England, daughter of King Henry VIII. The text as printed begins at page 891, since the book is only part of a much larger work. The transcriber kept its page numbers to ease finding entries in the index and glossary. An editor's note explains Du Wes's accent system.

Du Wes marked pronunciation with an accent under the vowel, and the editor moved it above, following modern usage, since Du Wes never used the upper accent. The book pairs English and French lines, with grace of God that I love so much set against its French twin. Readers get a rare Tudor language manual, in old spelling, made for a princess learning French.
29089-testimony-of-the-sonnets-as-to-the:
Jesse Johnson published this book in 1899 with G. P. Putnam's Sons, arguing that Shakespeare did not write the plays and poems credited to him. Johnson turns to the Sonnets themselves as evidence. He reads them literally, as a message from their author about his real feelings.

Johnson argues from the Sonnets' portrait of a young male friend and patron, and from an author past middle life, considerably older than Shakespeare was. Later chapters weigh Shakespeare's known life against the character shown in the Sonnets. Readers get a detailed case for the authorship question, valuable as a record of how fiercely readers debated Shakespeare's identity at the century's end.
29247-the-academic-questions-treatise-de:
C. D. Yonge translated these works of Cicero for George Bell and Sons in London in 1875. The volume gathers three major philosophical texts, with a sketch of the Greek philosophers Cicero mentions. Cicero, Rome's great orator, wrote philosophy in dialogue form, weighing Greek schools against each other.

The Academic Questions ask what we can know. The treatise De Finibus, on the chief good and evil, weighs pleasure, virtue, and duty across five books. The Tusculan Disputations cover contempt of death, bearing pain, grief of mind, other perturbations, and whether virtue alone suffices for a happy life. Readers get Cicero's philosophy in a clear Victorian translation, still a standard entry point.
31098-the-north-american-slime-moulds-a-:
Thomas H. Macbride's revised 1922 volume lists every species of slime mould, or Myxomycete, then reported from North America, with notes on some species from beyond the continent. First copyrighted in 1899, the book pairs formal descriptions with field observation, and it opens with verse epigraphs from Goethe and Batsch on the quiet wonder of these lowly growths.

Each entry helps a reader tell one form from another by its shape, color, and growth habit, making the book a working key for collectors and students of fungi-like organisms. It remains a record of what North American naturalists had found and named by the early twentieth century. It also records how they sorted a group that sits awkwardly between plant and animal life.
doe-osti-17014395-assessing-235u-prompt-: Double-checking uranium's neutron fingerprints got its DOE report, and this text validates the U-235 spectra against reaction rates. The analysis confirms the evaluations hold. Reactor math keeps its foundation. The check was completed. The foundation held. The check was DOE's.
doe-osti-3407904-deny-by-default-network: SPaRC got deny-by-default-secured, and this DOE bulletin covers network ports. The pages detail the technical findings. The security folks get their data. The bulletin was 002. The data were security. The SPaRC were ports. The 002 were bulletin. The network were ports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1009sp:
Understanding the Tax Reform Debate: Background, Criteria, and Questions, GAO-05-1009SP of September 1, 2005, is a guide to the fight over how the federal tax system should work. In 2005, Americans were to pay about $2.1 trillion in federal taxes. That sum was about 16.8 percent of gross domestic product.

The guide lays out why the system draws fire. Critics cite its drag on work, saving, and growth. They also cite unfair shares and hard rules that cost time to obey. It then frames the core choices: tax income or spending, and set flat or rising rates. Plain tests help readers judge any reform plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-193sp:
Social Security Reform: Answers to Key Questions, GAO-05-193SP of May 2, 2005, is a plain guide to a hard national choice. The program faces long-term cash strain. The longer the wait to act, the guide warns, the harder the fix will be. Each fix shifts what Americans pay in or draw out. Each one lands on the young as well as the old.

The guide boils the tangle down to the core picks. It tells how the program works now and how it began. It lays out its goals and how well it meets them. Deep values run through the text: shared duty, self-reliance, fairness, and respect.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-333sp:
National Airspace System, GAO-05-333SP of April 1, 2005, holds the pooled view of a panel of flight pros on a stuck upgrade. The air traffic build began in 1981. It has missed cost, time, and feat aims for more than two decades. On October 7, 2004, GAO brought the pros to one table. They came from firms, states, schools, and think tanks, here and abroad.

The panel named what they hold to blame for the long stall. They set out quick steps the new flight arm could take now. They set out long steps to lift the odds for the whole build. Their fields span safety, cost, and craft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-354sp:
Principles of Federal Appropriations Law: 2004 Update of the Third Edition, GAO-05-354SP of March 1, 2005, is a bound add-on to a famed law guide. Lawyers call the guide the Red Book. It tells how federal cash may be spent, and where the walls stand. Each year, a fresh add-on folds the past year's calls into the text.

This add-on covers calls from January 1 to December 31, 2004. It slips new text at set spots in Volume I of the third run. One such slip weighs a Supreme Court call on draft slips in laws. The full set posts each year on GAO's web site, under its legal goods.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-423sp:
Highlights of an Expert Panel, GAO-05-423SP of May 6, 2005, holds the pooled words of top travel pros on what road and rail cash buys. Travel shapes both the land's wealth and its daily life. Trips by folks and freight will grow, and vast sums must flow to keep the web sound. A lean federal purse and tight town cash force hard picks.

A House bill told GAO to weigh the gains and costs of each travel mode. The panel, of famed travel economists and hands from the whole land, forms part of that work. It met to trade views on how to count gains next to costs, mode by mode.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-578sp:
Expert views on the future of traditional pensions fill GAO-05-578SP, the highlights of a GAO forum issued on June 1, 2005. Defined benefit plans promise a set income in retirement. Many such plans, and the federal insurer behind them, have built up large deficits. Fewer workers hold these plans each year, as 401(k)-style plans spread. GAO gathered people who have shaped the pension debate to talk through what comes next.

The room mixed government officials, researchers, and accounting experts. Actuaries sat with plan sponsors, worker groups, and investors. Their charge reached past the deficits of single plans. The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, which insures the plans, faces strain of its own. Behind both sits a wider question: who should carry the risk of retirement income, workers or employers? The document records the forum's discussion, not a GAO audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-734sp:
A reference work, GAO-05-734SP (September 1, 2005), defines the terms used in the federal budget process. This fifth edition replaces a 1993 draft. GAO built it with the Treasury, the Office of Management and Budget, and the Congressional Budget Office. It serves Congress, agencies, and anyone who works with federal budget data.

The glossary sets out standard words for fiscal, budget, and program facts. Budget terms get the most space. Key economic and accounting terms are also defined. Where a word means one thing in budget work and another elsewhere, both senses are noted. Cross-references link related terms. Readers can use it to read budget files with a shared, steady vocabulary.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-739sp:
GAO-05-739SP, a reference paper dated May 2, 2005, explains two ways to judge federal programs. One way tracks set measures of results over time. The other runs deeper studies of how a program works. A 1993 law made agencies set goals and report each year on results. Both tools feed the budget process in Washington.

The paper defines each approach in plain terms. It then shows how the two fit together. Yearly reports are meant to carry both kinds of facts. Budget reviewers use both when they grade programs. First written in 1998, the paper rests on GAO work and study of the field. It gives staff a shared base for judging program results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-776sp:
GAO's own goals for the year ahead fill GAO-05-776SP, its performance plan dated June 1, 2005. The plan covers fiscal year 2006. It tells Congress and the public what the watchdog aims to do for them. It rests on a strategic plan for 2004 to 2009, issued in March 2004. That base plan was built in talks with members of Congress and other key parties.

The plan sets out how GAO will push toward its long-term goals. It follows the spirit of the federal results law that asks agencies to set goals and report on them. Readers can see the year's targets in one place. The plan also shows how yearly work ties to the five-year aims. It is a planning record, not an audit of an outside agency.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-796sp:
How to measure economic results was the theme of a GAO workshop summed up in GAO-05-796SP, dated July 18, 2005. GAO held the session on December 17, 2004. Experts discussed tools like benefit-cost analysis. Such tools can show whether a program gives good value. The aim was to take stock of current practice. Gaps and blocks in the use of these tools were also on the table.

The paper records what the group covered. It lays out where economic measures are used well and where they are not. It names the data and method issues that limit wider use. It also lists chances for agencies and scholars to improve the tools and the guidance behind them. Readers get a compact map of a technical field that shapes budget choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-832sp:
Federal pay design was debated at a symposium summed up in GAO-05-832SP, dated July 27, 2005. Five bodies convened the session on March 9, 2005. They included GAO and the federal personnel office. The topic was pay tied more to markets and to performance. Speakers came from public, private, and nonprofit groups. Each shared what worked and what proved hard.

The summary records the talks and the open debate that followed. Presenters described their own pay systems in detail. They covered design choices and day-to-day management. Stakeholders from across the personnel field took part. Readers get a range of tested models in one place. The record is meant to feed the wider debate on how federal pay should change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-958sp:
A plain guide to the government's yearly financial report is GAO-05-958SP, dated October 1, 2005. The United States government is the largest and most complex body on earth, the guide opens. Sound choices need financial facts that are useful, timely, and reliable. Treasury and the budget office build the yearly report together. The guide walks through its main parts.

The report gives a full overview of federal finances for Congress, executives, and citizens. News media and analysts who explain the data to the public are a key audience too. The guide explains what each main part of the report holds and why it matters. It flags big issues in how reliable the joined accounts are. Readers who find the yearly report dense get a map here. The aim is a comprehensive overview open to every American.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1sp:
GAO reports on its own record in GAO-06-1SP, its performance and accountability report for fiscal year 2005, issued on November 15, 2005. In the spirit of the Government Performance and Results Act, the report tells Congress and the public what the agency achieved. It pairs results data with the agency's financial statements. Outside auditors gave those statements a clean opinion. The clean result marks the 19th straight year for the agency.

The report walks through wins that GAO recommendations produced across government. Agency fixes at the Labor Department, NASA, and other bodies trace back to GAO advice. It also sets out how GAO measures its own performance and where it fell short. Few documents show a watchdog holding itself to its own rules. This one does, with audited figures and counted results. It is the agency's yearly account of itself to the taxpayers who fund it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-2sp:
GAO grades its own year in GAO-06-2SP, highlights published January 1, 2006. Fiscal 2005 was, by its account, an exceptional year. Auditors gave its books a clean opinion. It met or beat targets on 10 of 14 key measures. Three measures hit all-time records. It documented $39.6 billion in financial benefits. That is a return of $83 for each dollar it spent. It also counted over 1,400 nonfinancial benefits, a record.

Its work helped shape laws, including the 2004 intelligence reform act. Agencies and Congress acted on 85 percent of its recommendations. Two-thirds of its products that year carried advice, above target. The pages also track staff measures such as retention and satisfaction. Two hiring targets were missed narrowly, and the report says so. As self-reports go, this one names its shortfalls beside its wins. It models the accountability GAO demands from others.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-394sp:
How GAO works with foreign governments and audit offices is set down here. GAO-06-394SP, a January 31, 2006 special publication, contains GAO's international protocols. The protocols govern GAO work with international parts or effects. They state clear policies for contact with U.S. agencies, other national governments, and international organizations. They also tell supreme audit institutions what to expect from GAO.

The rules aim to cover most cases that arise in such work. They match, where fitting, the protocols for GAO work with Congress and federal agencies. Readers get the ground rules in plain form. The publication is a reference, not a program review. It shows how GAO keeps its overseas work open and steady.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-533sp:
Buying from a shrinking, global supplier base was the theme of a one-day forum. Special publication GAO-06-533SP, dated March 31, 2006, gives highlights of that forum. GAO sponsored the forum in October 2005. Defense policy experts took part. They came from federal agencies, defense industry, nonprofit groups, and academia. Talks were held on a non-attribution basis to reach consensus.

Agencies face changing threats, fast-moving technology, and tight budgets. Contractors now take on more program management work. The government staff who oversee buying have shrunk. The forum sought the top challenges in managing suppliers. Readers get agreed themes, not a GAO audit finding. The title names the topic plainly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-551sp:
Who serves on civil rights advisory panels in each state is counted here. Special publication GAO-06-551SP, dated May 1, 2006, analyzes the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights' state advisory committees. There are 51 such committees. They feed state and local civil rights information to the commission. GAO presents data on member demographics and occupations. Data came from the most recent charter for each committee.

State comparison data came from census figures. Religion data came from a 2001 survey and political data from a 2004 study, both named in the text. Work ran from April 2005 to March 2006. Readers can see how committee membership reflects varied criteria. A companion report is cited.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-734sp:
Survey results from first-round Enterprise Communities fill GAO-06-734SP, a data report GAO issued on September 22, 2006. The communities were designated in 1994 under the Empowerment Zone and Enterprise Community program. Each received program grants, and local businesses could use a tax-exempt bond. GAO surveyed the communities to record how they ran the program. The survey is a companion to GAO's wider audit of the program's results.

The tables report answers from community leaders on their core tasks. Large shares said residents helped set priorities and sat on governing boards. About nine in ten said they gathered facts on community needs from residents. The report presents these self-reported figures without judging program success. Researchers can use it to see how the model worked on the ground.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-759sp:
A conference on disabled youths moving into work or college is summed up in GAO-06-759SP, a summary GAO issued on June 20, 2006. Federal programs invest heavily in transition services for youths with disabilities. Research shows these youths are less likely than peers to move smoothly from high school to jobs or further study. GAO brought together experts and practitioners in California to share what works. The summary records the views voiced at that meeting.

Panelists agreed that real challenges exist in two key areas. They said the school system, as they knew it in California, gave too little training in job and life skills. Transition preparation also fell short for many students. Speakers valued academic study, yet urged a stronger practical track. The summary gives program managers a ground-level view of the gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-81sp:
A survey of housing bias complainants is published in GAO-06-81SP, a companion document dated October 31, 2005. It supports GAO's report on how the Department of Housing and Urban Development resolves discrimination complaints. For that study, GAO ran a telephone survey of a sample of complainants. Their cases had been investigated and closed by federal or partner agency offices. This document reproduces the survey in annotated form, question by question.

The annotations explain how each question was asked and how answers were counted. They also give the response figures, with notes on sampling error. Readers can judge for themselves how complainants rated the process. As a methods record, the document shows the evidence base behind the main report's findings. It is a reference for anyone who studies complaint handling.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-931sp:
Stronger powers for federal inspectors general are weighed in a GAO panel summary, GAO-06-931SP, dated September 11, 2006. The Inspector General Act of 1978 set up these in-house watchdogs. They audit, probe, and hunt fraud in their own agencies, with rights to records, staff, and subpoenas.

A Senate panel asked if a 2005 bill, H.R. 2489, would sharpen that freedom. Its terms set fixed terms and removal rules, direct budget paths, and a joint council. GAO's panel also weighed pay, credentials, and past advice to merge some offices. The summary frames how watchdog freedom can grow without losing grip.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1080sp:
State and local budgets face lasting strain in the next decade, GAO projects in a study paper, GAO-07-1080SP, dated July 18, 2007. For over a decade GAO models have shown federal deficits driven by aging and health costs, on a path its chief called imprudent and unsustainable. Towns and states give many daily services, and lean on federal grants.

GAO built a model of the whole state and local sector. It projects income and spending to 2050, if current policies hold. The data come from national income accounts. The model treats the sector as a whole, not any one state. Its point is scope: the fiscal squeeze is national, not just federal.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1155sp:
Health care 20 years ahead is the theme of a GAO forum summary, GAO-07-1155SP, dated September 7, 2007. Rising health costs, the Comptroller General has warned, will strain the federal budget and the wider economy if the system is not fixed. A forum at GAO on May 17, 2007 took up that long view.

Health policy experts, business heads, and officials debated cost, access, and quality. Talks were led by known economists and health care figures, with a keynote at lunch. At the close, players were polled with live, private voting gear. The paper gives the highlights, and the poll picks, as a guide to steps that can be taken today.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-117sp:
Two ways to state the federal deficit are set side by side in a GAO primer, GAO-07-117SP, dated December 1, 2006. The cash deficit works like a checkbook: money in, money out. It drives budget debate and tracks near-term borrowing. The accrual measure counts costs when they are incurred, even if paid years later.

Pensions and retiree health care show up in the accrual view, but not the cash one. GAO tells how the two sums are alike, and how they differ. It names what drives gaps between them. Used together, GAO argues, they give a fuller picture of the nation's fiscal state, today and long term.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1210sp:
A collapsed bridge span in Minneapolis in August 2007 sharpened debate over the nation's transportation network. GAO-07-1210SP, dated September 19, 2007, presents highlights of a forum GAO convened on that policy. Experts from government, universities, and industry joined GAO's own specialists. They weighed the goals of national transportation policy and the federal role in meeting them. They also took up how to pay for those goals.

Participants said national policy had lost focus over time. They ranked better mobility and global competitiveness as the top goals. Many urged clear goals tied to performance measures that show real results. Such measures, they said, should drive federal funding choices. The group also pressed for tools that help local agencies plan and judge their own systems. The highlights note that the views are the forum's, not GAO's own position.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1sp:
GAO's own strategic plan for fiscal years 2007 through 2012 is numbered GAO-07-1SP and dated March 30, 2007. GAO updates the plan at least once every 3 years. The law on government performance calls for such updates. The plan sets out the goals and methods GAO will use to serve Congress. It names the bodies of work GAO expects Congress to request.

The plan is framed by hard national problems. It cites the large and growing long-term fiscal imbalance. It cites rising strain in paying for health care for an aging public. Homeland security and defense change efforts fill much of the expected workload. The plan also notes lessons from Hurricanes Katrina and Rita and the risk of a flu pandemic. GAO presents the themes that will shape its audits and reviews. They include security threats, fiscal sustainability, and global interdependence.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-289sp:
By law, GAO must report each year on how it used special personnel powers Congress granted it. The account appears in GAO-07-289SP, dated December 1, 2006. It forms Appendix 2 of GAO's 2006 performance report. Two laws supply the powers and the reporting duty. They are the GAO Personnel Flexibilities Act of 2000 and the GAO Human Capital Reform Act of 2004. The provisions cover early retirement offers and buyout payments. They also cover layoff rules and senior executive matters.

The report walks through each provision in turn. It states which powers GAO used in the period and which it left idle. The 2004 act made the early retirement and buyout powers permanent. It kept the same reporting terms for them. For the short window before that act took hold, GAO reports no use of its revised layoff rules. The document is a compliance record for Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-2sp:
Once a year, the government's own watchdog reports on its performance to Congress and the public. The fiscal year 2006 account is GAO-07-2SP, dated November 15, 2006. The report follows the format of the Government Performance and Results Act. It covers what GAO's audits achieved that year. It presents the agency's financial statements and performance data. GAO states that both are complete and reliable.

The year set records, the report says. GAO's work produced $51 billion in financial benefits. That is a $105 return for each dollar Congress gave the agency. GAO also counted 1,342 nonfinancial benefits, like better services and changed laws. Its executives testified at 240 hearings. Independent auditors gave GAO's books a clean opinion. That marks the 20th straight year without a qualification. The report also samples major audits across its goal areas.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-308sp:
As Washington rewrote its Iraq strategy, GAO packaged its oversight findings for the new Congress. The papers form GAO-07-308SP, dated January 9, 2007. They rest on 67 Iraq reports and testimonies issued since May 2003. Iraq had held three elections and seated an elected government. Yet violence grew through 2006, the papers say. The set covers six areas. They are strategy and costs, security, and governance. Reconstruction, troop readiness, and contract outcomes complete the list.

Attacks rose all through 2006 despite more trained Iraqi troops, GAO notes. Absence and split loyalties limited those forces. U.S. troops faced rising casualties and worn gear. Readiness and reserve supply both suffered. Iraq's economy grew, and some services were restored. But graft, joblessness, and weak services persisted. Ministries failed to spend capital budgets in full. The papers urge sustained U.S. and world support. They frame questions for oversight of the revised strategy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-341sp:
The federal deficit looks different depending on the accounting lens, and this update tracks both views. GAO-07-341SP, dated January 22, 2007, refreshes figures for fiscal year 2006. It updates an earlier study of cash and accrual deficits. The cash view counts money in and out. The accrual view, called net operating cost, counts costs when incurred. GAO warns against leaning on any single year's exact figures.

Both deficits shrank in 2006, GAO reports. The cash deficit fell by about $70 billion. The accrual deficit fell by over $300 billion. The wider accrual drop drives the update's analysis. GAO also repeats a standing caveat. For the 10th straight year, the government could not prove the reliability of large parts of its financial report. The update draws its data from that report. It is meant to be read with the earlier study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-362sp:
This short GAO publication asks Americans to face the government's true balance sheet. It is GAO-07-362SP, dated January 31, 2007. The booklet explains the federal financial condition in plain terms. It also lays out the long-term fiscal outlook. Its stated aim is to help Congress and citizens judge both. Total federal liabilities stood near $10,413 billion at September 30, 2006.

Gross federal debt forms the largest single piece of those liabilities. The booklet draws its figures from the fiscal year 2006 financial report. It argues the nation is not well set for this century's tests. Fiscal responsibility to future generations is its core theme. Current policy, it says, fails that stewardship duty. The publication pairs the present snapshot with long-range projections.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-3sp: The watchdog's 2006 report card arrived in 2007, and GAO's highlights booklet grades its own performance and accountability. The document touts the wins. The highlights show the auditor auditing itself in public. The self-grade was posted for all to see. The mirror was held up in public.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-406sp: The Pentagon's wish list got its annual grade in 2007 — GAO's booklet assesses the selected weapon programs one by one. The findings size up the costs and schedules. The report reads as the buyer's guide nobody at the Pentagon wanted to write.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-421sp: The watchdog's 2008 game plan arrived in 2007, and GAO's performance plan lays out the goals for the coming fiscal year. The document sets the targets in writing. The plan shows the auditor holding itself to a public promise. The auditor's promise was written for all to see.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-45sp: Federal buying's big problems got a GAO forum in 2007, and the highlights booklet distills the acquisition challenges and opportunities. The text captures the debate. The guide shows the procurement world talking through its troubles. The forum aired the issues. The buying debate was aired fully.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-467sp: The forces shaping America's future got a GAO briefing in 2007 — the booklet distills the themes from the agency's five-year strategic plan. The findings look ahead to the coming challenges. The report reads as the watchdog's weather forecast for the nation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-517sp: Older drivers were the road-safety frontier in 2007 — GAO's survey checks how the states took up the federal highway advice. The findings grade the uptake state by state. The report treads gently: keep grandma behind the wheel, but keep everyone safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-801sp: Afghanistan was the other war in 2007 — GAO's booklet frames the key oversight questions for securing and rebuilding the country. The highlights bundle the hard issues for Congress in one place. The report reads as the quiet warning sounding beside Iraq's loud debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-127sp: This 2007 GAO booklet bottles the best of a forum on gauging America's natural wealth — land, water, and wild systems — and whether the nation is living off the interest or eating the principal. Experts hashed out how to score nature's health in hard numbers. The highlights give Congress a starter kit for thinking green in budget terms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1sp: The watchdog grades itself in this 2007 yearly report. GAO tallies its audits, its wins, and the tax dollars its tips saved — then opens its own books for all to see. The report holds the audit agency to the same plain standard it sets for others: show your work, own your misses, and prove you earned your keep.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-2sp: GAO published its findings on GAO Performance and Accountability Highlights: Fiscal Year 2007 in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-386sp: GAO published its findings on federal User Fees: A Design Guide in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports. The library keeps it as part of the public record.

lincoln-an-account-of-his-personal-life-:
Nathaniel Wright Stephenson studies Lincoln's own life in this book. His subtitle stresses the springs of Lincoln's acts. The ordeal of war revealed and deepened those springs, he argues. Stephenson thanks William Roscoe Thayer for John Hay's manuscript diary.

Helen Nicolay confirmed points from the official life for him. Lincoln's last living secretary, Colonel Stoddard, gave kind aid. Henry Johnson found Lincoln's work as a lawyer in a slave case. Judge Marshall checked and filled out that curious case for the book. A futile search for Republican committee papers also aided his certainty. Professor Ulrich Phillips helped the Chandler inquiries generously. Plain talk and close facts mark Stephenson's approach to his subject throughout.
nasa-tm-19660014179-scientific-basis-of-:
Alexander G Smith of the University of Florida gave this address in January 1966 on observing the universe from space, issued as a Marshall memorandum on March 24, 1966. His subtitle names applications of orbiting platforms and space probes in radio astronomy. Jupiter is named in the catalog note as a source of data for such work. From orbit, instruments escape the limits of Earth's air.

Smith lays out the scientific basis for that move. Radio waves from planets and stars carry facts no other signal can give. Probes can also go to the source, rather than wait for its signals. The address captures the case for space astronomy just as its first great observatories were being planned.
nasa-tm-19690008665-diurnal-and-seasonal:
H. C. Brinton, R. A. Pickett, and H. A. Taylor Jr. of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this October 1968 preprint, X-621-68-375. They report daily and seasonal changes in the ion mix of the topside ionosphere, measured by an ion mass spectrometer aboard Explorer 32. The satellite sampled the charged layer from low heights to far above Earth.

The team found ion patterns tied directly to the Sun's angle in the sky. At one northern height, oxygen ions rose sharply at dawn and ruled the daytime layer. Hydrogen ions ruled at night instead, far stronger than by day. Seasonal contrasts between summer and winter hemispheres showed in the oxygen and nitrogen patterns. Hydrogen and helium changed far less across the seasons.
